Work out the language proposal a rung needs, before it is worth making. Each proposal must be a defect in something that exists or an extension to a clause already required, never a new subsystem.

```day-atom
{"in":["filed-gap","architecture-record"],"out":["rfc-set"],"next":[],"done":["rfc-set"]}
```

Words for concepts; symbols only where the symbol is the concept. Kept: -> for function type, => for match, |x| for closure, ! for the effect row, operators. This retired two earlier proposals — arrows for interference and for protocol direction — both glyphs invented to dodge a collision that abbreviation had caused. Symbol space is small and adversarial; word space is not.

Surface decisions recorded in docs/rfcs/000-surface-conventions.md: effects move to the arrow as ! on their own line; interference groups in a concurrent block with asks/promises, and those words outside the block must be a parse error; region becomes shared; protocols name what an endpoint offers with provides/uses rather than dual or client/server; opacity is discharged per obligation with by unfold(f) rather than a function-level clause; opaque and linearity are keywords not attributes; spec fn gains ensures so a sealed predicate has an interface.

Bulla's RFCs drop their numbers and use slugs. The numbers collided head-on with Thermite's own, which are allocated in its GitHub issues: RFC-1 is issue #2 (Thermite 2), RFC-2 is #119 (the certification surface), RFC-3 is #120 (versioning). Our 001-003 sat on all three, and docs/assurance-model.md cites upstream's RFC-2 while this directory held a different one under the same name. Renumbering into the same sequence moves the collision rather than removing it, because two authorities allocating from one counter is what produced it. A document filed upstream gains its number there and keeps its slug locally. Mapping recorded in docs/rfcs/README.md. Two retitles are forced by the resource decision: RFC-003 Resource invariants becomes shared-state-invariants, RFC-004 Linear types becomes resource-types.

What a mutant of an asks clause is, answered. Mutation scores a contract by mutating the body, and the two interference clauses sit on opposite sides of that. 'promises' scores like 'ensures' - a body mutant violating the guarantee is killed by it - with one dependency: the observable must include the effect trace on shared state rather than only the return value, which is equivalent-mutants.md OQ-2 and currently out of scope since v0.1 scores fx pure bodies. 'asks' has no body mutant at all, because it is a claim about the environment, and silence from a scorer reads as a pass. Two hazards need two probes: an unnecessary rely is caught by weakening it to 'asks nothing' and seeing whether the obligation still discharges, which is a strengthening probe; an unjustified rely is caught only at the composition site, where every peer's promises must imply it. The second has no home today, so an asks is a free assumption checked against nothing - the same shape as write(a_resource_that_does_not_exist) certifying at L3. Consequence for the assurance model: an undischarged asks carries a weaker boundary coordinate and the per-clause tuple must say so.

Three mechanisms added. LOCK SCOPE: '! owns(r)' makes the function body the critical section, which reduces the new rule to two clauses that already exist - the guarded type's invariant becomes an implicit requires at entry and ensures at exit, assumed nowhere between. No new construct, no proof block, no statement-level annotation, which matters because Thermite has none. Stated cost: a critical section is always a whole function, so holding a lock for part of a body means factoring that part out; the gain is that every critical section's extent is visible in a signature. The conflict rule gains three rows: owns(r) || owns(r) accepts because the lock serialises them, while owns(r) || write(r) and owns(r) || read(r) both reject, because runtime exclusion holds between holders of the lock and says nothing about a function that never takes it - and that function is the one the static rule has to stop. LINEARITY CONTAGION: a struct or enum reachable to a resource type is itself a resource, declared and checked rather than inferred, because inference would make dropability invisible at the declaration. Covers enums (an empty variant does not exempt the type), generic carriers (Result<Grant,_> and Vec<Grant>, load-bearing because allocate returns Result<(Allocator,Grant),u64> and the error path is where a grant goes missing), upward only, and destructuring as consumption of the container that hands back each part as its own obligation. Not reachable until G4 lifts. CHANNELS AS SHARED STATE: a channel is shared state whose discipline is the protocol type rather than the effect row, since the type names one sender per step. Three requirements follow: endpoints must be resources rather than affine, because duplication puts two parties at one step and dropping abandons the peer mid-session; the row carries only 'blocks'; and an endpoint may not be stored in shared state, which is the restriction the other two rest on.

Lock scope supports both forms, and the combination is better than either. The row declares which locks a function takes; a holding block declares where. Four rules: owns(r) with no block means the body is the section, so function scope is the sugar; a holding r block requires owns(r) in the row, by the same mechanism that puts asks inside interleaves; the row is an upper bound, so a block under an if is fine; and two or more owns atoms require blocks, because a bare row leaves the acquisition order unstated and cannot be cleared for deadlock. Two objections I had raised were wrong. Flow-sensitivity: a holding block is lexical, so the extent is syntactic and reentrancy is containment rather than dataflow - that would only bite with separate acquire and release statements. Ordering: function scope alone CANNOT express the order its own open question asks for, since ! owns(a), owns(b) does not say which is taken first, while nested blocks state it structurally. So blocks are what make a region partial order checkable rather than a convenience that complicates it. Cost: the implicit requires/ensures reduction covers only the whole-body case; the block needs one derived obligation at its edges, deriving from the lock ... guards ... declaration rather than from new clause syntax.

Linearity is on the type rather than the binding, with an explicit escape. The binding form is closer to the substrate, since Verus's tracked is a mode on a binding rather than a property of a type, so the lowering inserts tracked at each use. The type wins because contagion is not optional and only types can state it: a field is not a binding, so 'a struct with a resource field is a resource' has nothing to attach to under the binding reading. The flexibility given up is returned by forget(g), which discharges the obligation without consuming the resource and records forgets(r) as a state effect on the region it came from - so the escape exists, is counted, appears in every transitive caller's row by the composition law, and can be refused by a release rule the way TMK refuses #[boundary]. This also converts the panic hole into a stateable choice: an abort performing an implicit forget is either declared as forgets(r) for every live resource, or refused in a release build.

The surface-conventions document had no migration section, the same defect just fixed in the effect-rows document, and its break is larger: all 567 clause sites across 69 files and 155 items (ens 208, req 160, fx 150, dec 31, inv 18), plus 110 trivial clauses changing spelling. Three things make it affordable anyway. It is mechanical - a rename plus a fixed reorder is a deterministic source-to-source rewrite, so the tool is a parser and a printer rather than an analysis, where the effect-rows migration cannot be automated because deciding which region an alloc belongs to is a judgement about what the program shares. The one non-mechanical part is small: a naive rewriter emits 'requires true' rather than 'requires nothing', which stays legal, so sugar adoption is an optional second pass over 110 sites rather than a correctness condition. And certificates survive: the .cert.json oracle subset is item/level/tautology/vacuous_precondition/effects/slag, with clause names appearing nowhere, verified across the corpus. The contrast belongs to the other document - effects IS in the oracle subset, so the effect-row systematization invalidates certificates, affecting 1 of the 12 oracle items carrying an effects field because it carries alloc.

Two revisions. PROTOCOLS: the body names roles as bare nouns with a block each, and the signature conjugates the role into a verb - protocol PageRequest repeats { user { op, count }, provider { status, base } } with fn pager(c: provides PageRequest). The proposed uses{}/provides{} pair was rejected because the two words are not symmetric in meaning: both roles SEND at their turns, and 'uses' reads as consuming rather than sending. Nouns in the body because there is no single subject there, verbs in the signature because the function is the subject, which is the clause-grammar rule applied where it applies. The floating 'end,' is gone: closing the braces ends the session, and 'repeats' in the header says it loops, which is the common case for a long-lived server and puts the fact where a reader meets it first. LOCKS: there is no whole-body default. owns(r) requires a holding r block, always. The reason is the honest-row principle one level down - an implicit whole-body scope makes an over-declared lock invisible, since owns(r) with no block is indistinguishable from 'I meant the whole body', so a lock declared and never taken reads as correct. It also makes acquisition order structural in every case rather than only when two locks are present.

Defect found in the worked examples: the surface-conventions and protocol-types documents carried the same protocol with its two steps in opposite orders, so one described a pager that responds before it receives a request. In a session type the order of steps is the semantics. Dates to the original naming brainstorm in the previous session and was carried forward unnoticed through every revision until a full worked example put the two side by side.

The panic question in resource types needs no new rule, and the resolution is a principle rather than a policy. A resource binding is consumed on every path THAT RETURNS, scoped exactly as ensures is and for the same reason: a function that aborts does not establish its postcondition either, and nobody calls that a hole in ensures. The resource obligation is postcondition-shaped and inherits the scoping. The static check already gets it right without being told, because an aborting call diverges and the code after it is unreachable, which is why Rust's move checker does not demand consumption after panic!(). The language also already prices non-returning paths: diverge drops an item from L3 to L1, total to partial correctness, precisely because postconditions are claims about returning executions. Cost: one word of precision in the guarantee - exactly once on every path that returns, not exactly once unconditionally. The two cases stay distinct: an abort is fatal with no subsequent state and needs no operation, while teardown is deliberate, on a returning path, and is forget(g), counted in the row and refusable by a release rule. Tearing down a faulted partition is the second case, which is what motivated forget to begin with.

The 'region partial order' was two different orders, and the two documents had been deferring to each other as though it were one. CONTAINMENT (effect rows) is a tree derived from the type structure - if SchedState has a field runqueue then scheduler.runqueue is a sub-region - and conflict is ancestry: write(scheduler) conflicts with read(scheduler.runqueue), while sibling sub-regions are disjoint and compose concurrently. It needs no new declaration form because containment follows the type, and it is blocked on G4 since a declared type cannot be a field today. It is what makes per-CPU heaps expressible, which is the fix for allocation serialising once alloc becomes write(heap). ACQUISITION (shared state) is a declared rank, 'lock sched_lock guards SchedState at 1', with nesting requiring a strictly increasing rank and equal ranks never nested. Because a holding block is lexical the check is a comparison over block nesting rather than an analysis. A total rank is stricter than necessary and is sound and cheap; declaration order was rejected because reordering declarations would silently change which programs are legal. One rule falls out that a rank alone does not catch: if any function in handlers{} carries owns(r), every normal-context function carrying owns(r) must also carry owns(interrupts), or the handler deadlocks against the code it preempted on its own CPU. That is among the most common concurrency defects in real kernels and it is checkable from the rows plus the handler declaration.

The numeric lock rank is dropped. Numbers are arbitrary, carry no reason, force renumbering on insertion, and collide when two people add locks independently. Replaced by a two-part rule. DEFAULT: a function holds at most one lock at a time, so no order is declared because there is no nesting to order, and the whole deadlock-by-ordering class is gone by construction; the check is counting active holding blocks. WHEN NESTING IS NEEDED: the order is relative - lock frame_lock guards FrameTable after sched_lock - which names the relationship rather than a coordinate, yields a DAG (the partial order actually wanted, where a total rank was over-strong), detects cycles at declaration rather than at a use site, and makes adding a lock one line with nothing renumbered. Inference from whole-program usage was considered and rejected: the order would become whatever was written first, a library could not state what callers must do, and a violation would surface as a cycle spanning modules rather than a local mistake. The staging matters - the restriction ships first and 'after' is what lifts it, which keeps the mechanism tied to a case that exists, and today there is no verified subsystem so there are zero examples of a genuine two-lock critical section. The masking rule is unaffected because both functions in that scenario take only one lock.

Protocol syntax settled, superseding two earlier drafts. A protocol is a SEQUENCE of turns, each labelled with the role whose turn it is, ending in 'end': protocol PageRequest { User { op, count }, Provider { status, base }, end }. Roles are NAMES not keywords, so a protocol names its own roles in its own domain, and they are capitalised because they are types. Endpoints are paths: PageRequest::Provider, replacing 'provides P' and 'uses P'. Two reasons the path form wins. It is a noun in a TYPE position where the subject is c rather than the function - c does not provide anything, it IS an endpoint - so the verb form violated the same clause-grammar rule it was chosen to satisfy. And it generalises: Transfer::Coordinator is well-formed for any number of roles, where two verbs cannot name three parties. 'end' is the last element of the sequence rather than a marker after it, which is what it is in the theory where a session type is !T . ?U . end. A 'repeats' header flag was tried and withdrawn because real repetition is conditional - a server loops until told to close - so termination is a branch, 'repeat | end'. A branch costs a message: the choice must be transmitted or the peer waits forever, so repeat|end implies a discriminant on the wire sent by whichever party acts next. Termination is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: an endpoint is a resource that must be consumed exactly once, and running the protocol to completion is what consumes it, so a protocol that never ends has an endpoint that can never be released.

Binary sessions are specified as a DEGENERATE GLOBAL TYPE rather than as a pair of dual local types, and this is the load-bearing framing choice. Duality is a binary operation and does not generalise: with three roles there is no 'the dual', and pairwise duality does not compose - three pairwise-dual channels can deadlock in a cycle with every pairwise check passing. The multiparty answer (Honda, Yoshida, Carbone 2008) replaces duality with PROJECTION: write one global type, project onto each role for that role's local type, check each implementation against its own projection, so consistency holds by construction because all local types come from one source. Under that framing PageRequest::Provider IS the projection G restricted to Provider, and for two roles projection coincides with duality. Specifying binary this way costs nothing now and means a later multiparty extension adds cases to a function rather than replacing the framing; specifying it as duality would have to be thrown away. What multiparty needs is both parties named per step, which is a notation change and where the arrow earns its way back since A -> B is a labelled edge whose symbol is the concept. Deadlock freedom is free for binary and not for multiparty: duality gives it structurally for two, while a well-formed global type gives communication safety, protocol fidelity and progress within one session, but cyclic waits across interleaved sessions need more.

Editor support written, and Thermite has none upstream - tooling/ holds gates and registries and nothing that makes a .th file readable. Three artifacts in tooling/editor/: a Vim syntax file plus ftdetect, and a TextMate grammar for VS Code, Sublime and anything TextMate-shaped. Claude Code itself has no custom-grammar support, so the terminal renders our 56 thermite fenced blocks unhighlighted; retagging them rust was considered and rejected because it would give fn keyword colour while rendering requires, ensures, keeps and resource as ordinary identifiers, which miscolours the clause vocabulary in a language whose thesis is that misread clauses yield vacuous proofs. Highlighting choices carry the design: clauses get Statement, the strongest group, because the clause vocabulary is what the language is for; the effect row gets PreProc because it is type-level rather than a predicate and should not read like one; parameterised atoms match only where applied, so write(heap) in a row is an effect and a write elsewhere is an identifier. Verified by probing synID groups in vim against the tour file rather than by eye.

The effect algebra is written as its own cross-cutting document. An effect label denotes an algebraic theory - a signature of operations plus equations - and a row is a set of them; each label owes a theory, a composition law, and a COMMUTATION fact, and the third is what makes the conflict table a theorem rather than an axiom. The admissibility criterion is that a primitive is admissible when it generates a frame condition expressible in the prover's logic, which is a real filter: it removed exception and kept random as an atom, neither by taste. Basis: state(r), accrues(M), exception, partiality, io(sigma) generate frame conditions; random and blocks are given atoms that do not. A row entry is a theory instance plus the operations used, so read(r) is state(r)/{get} and write(r) is state(r)/{get,put}, and the DRF table falls out of which operation pairs commute - including the case nobody would have guessed, that random || random accepts because independent samples commute. exception leaves the basis because Thermite has no unwinding (probed: no catch/try/throw/raise in the surface, panic is exit 101, wrappers are total), so a recoverable failure is decided at the call site and belongs in the type as Result<T,M> with M a monoid. random stays as an atom meaning 'I claim nothing about this value', which is sound and does not support uniformity or unpredictability; a PRNG is state(entropy) and the stipulation is what makes predictable-PRNG incompatibilities visible. irq is not a primitive: it decomposes into the handler as environment, masking as owns(interrupts), and one platform assumption about handler atomicity. handlers{} declares a preemption order with normal context at level 0, generating promises(h) implies asks(g) only where level(h) > level(g), and handlers are roots of the call graph so effect propagation terminates there.

Loop clauses go before the body brace, not inside it. Inside the braces they read as statements and blend into the first real statement of the loop body. The principled version: a function's clauses sit between its signature and its body, so a loop's clauses sit between its head and its body - 'while cond keeps ... measures ... { body }'. This is not a design change but a correction of drift on my part: the current language already does it this way, verified by probe, since 'while i < n inv i <= n dec n - i { i = i + 1; }' certifies at L3. The surface-conventions worked example and the Thermite 3 tour had both drifted to putting them inside.

Thermite 3 is written as the sequencing document, with a syntax-only anchor. The name borrows upstream's own generational convention from RFC-1 'Thermite 2' rather than coining one, and the framing is that Thermite 3 is a SURFACE generation where Thermite 2 was a semantics one - which is what makes the expensive-to-review and cheap-to-review parts separable so the cheap one can go first. THE ANCHOR changes no expressive power at all: req/ens/inv/dec renamed, fx becoming the ! row moved first, the clause order fixed, conjunct blocks as sugar for &&, and 'requires nothing' as sugar for true. Everything that adds an obligation, a type or a check is out of it. One deliberate exception recorded: alloc and rand are abbreviations the throughline would rename, and the anchor leaves them alone because the effect-rows RFC turns them into write(heap) and write(entropy) anyway and renaming a token twice is churn. Four reasons it goes first: separately evaluable, so a maintainer can accept better clause names without evaluating six feature proposals; it anchors the rest so later proposals are written in the settled surface rather than re-arguing naming; highest value per risk, since rejection is learned early and cheaply; and mechanical, 567 sites, a deterministic rewrite with certificates surviving. It is also a version-number event, which connects it to live upstream RFC-3 on what a version number promises. SEQUENCE: defects, then the RFC process (Thermite's only RFC namespace is its issue tracker, which cannot version a document), then the anchor, then the effect algebra, then the rungs in order. Readiness: eight documents ready, the crash clause not - it is parked for a Bulla reason that does not transfer and the crash model is the real blocker.

The anchor is written as its own proposable document, full-words-anchor.md, rather than living as a table in the sequencing document and reasoning mixed into the surface conventions. The two are doing different jobs: surface-conventions is the design record carrying every decision with its reasoning including rejected candidates, and is what our own RFCs assume; the anchor is a PROPOSAL - self-contained, minimal, with a migration - and it does not need the rejected linearity candidates because linearity is not in it. So it is a new document rather than a split, and it is much smaller: the governing principle, the clause-grammar rule that justifies keeps and measures as names, the six changes, the ordering rule, the migration numbers, the address-segment constraint, and an explicit list of what is excluded. Nothing about resource, forget, interleaves, protocols or the effect algebra appears in it. The exclusion list is deliberately long so the proposal can be short.

The Thermite 3 document becomes a full language specification rather than a sequencing note. Read top to bottom it specifies the surface; read the status column it is a roadmap. Fourteen sections - functions, clauses, the effect row, specification vocabulary, data, resources, shared state, locks, interference, interrupts, protocols, loops, durability, and where it is going - each with syntax, a one-line meaning, a status mark (anchor / rung N / research), and a link to the document that carries its design. The status marks are what make one document serve both purposes: 'anchor' means it is in the syntax-only change and costs no expressive power, 'rung N' places it on the ladder, 'research' means the surface is reachable and the discharge open. Section 14 shows the research surface in syntax - random(Uniform) for distributional effects and cost(180) discharged rather than declared - so a reader can see where the language is going rather than only where it is. The rollout half keeps the sequence, the dependency tree drawn as a graph, per-document readiness, and the staged ask on a maintainer.

The crash clause's parking reason is corrected and the real gate named. The document said it was unscheduled because nothing in Bulla has durable state, which is true and is OURS - it does not transfer to Thermite, whose own examples/editor/editor.th is a verified editor carrying read(input), write(output), alloc, diverge, term. That is a program that writes files, in the examples directory, today, and an editor that dies mid-save guarantees nothing about the file. The corpus also carries write(db), write(log) and net(db). So the upstream case is one clause shaped like ensures, settled metatheory, and existing programs that need it. What actually gates it is the CRASH MODEL: which writes survive and in what order depends on the device and the barriers issued, so it is a per-device assumption that must be stated as plainly as the machine model. A first model is now stated so the assumption is concrete - synchronous and sector-atomic, where a write is atomic at sector granularity and durable when it returns, which is enough for the journalling obligation and is NOT true of a real disk since devices buffer and reorder. Saying so is the point: it holds only for a device driven with a flush after every write, which makes it a trusted input with a name rather than a fact about hardware. The asynchronous model where a location maps to a set of possible values until a barrier collapses it is the next model rather than a different mechanism, and the clause does not change. Consequence for the assurance model: a survives clause closes at the crash model rather than at the program, so its tuple needs a coordinate naming which model was assumed, the way to_platform(p) names a platform.

The RFC-process proposal for Thermite, settled. RFCs become files at .design/rfcs/NNNN-slug.md with front matter carrying rfc, title, status, supersedes, introduces, and optionally discussion. Four properties fix what issues cannot do: one PR per RFC so review is line-by-line on the document; always merge and never close, so a rejected RFC keeps its reasoning; introduces feeds the REQ registry so implementation status is DERIVED rather than declared and cannot drift; and issues go back to being defect reports. Versions are derived from git - one commit per edit, cited as 'RFC-4 r3 @ a1b2c3d' where the revision is the commit count on the file - so there is no version field for the same reason there is no implemented status. A consequence stated rather than discovered: an RFC PR should not be squash-merged or its review history collapses. NUMBERING: a draft's number is provisional and merging makes it canonical, with no extra field because status: draft already means it. Take the next free number when writing so the RFC is citable during the argument; if two drafts collide or a reviewer wants a different slot, the number moves at merge and the file is renamed. The gate enforces the distinction: two non-draft RFCs sharing a number is an error, a draft colliding with a non-draft is an error, two drafts sharing is reported and not fatal. MIGRATION: all four existing RFCs move, renumbered chronologically, because #17 was filed second and never numbered - so unnumbered becomes RFC-2, the old RFC-2 (#119) becomes 3, the old RFC-3 (#120) becomes 4, and the process RFC takes 5. Renumbering is done once and never again; it is affordable now because nothing in the tree and no issue or PR body references RFC-2 or RFC-3, checked. #17 is also the proposal's own best argument: it is an RFC that proposed the canonical REQ registry, shipped, and was never numbered, so an RFC that built the requirement-tracking system is itself untracked.

The RFC-process proposal is filed as Thermite PR #127, with the four existing RFCs migrated and renumbered chronologically. Contents: .design/rfcs/0001-thermite-2.md through 0005-rfc-process.md, tooling/rfc-check.py with a --index mode deriving versions from git, three requirements added to registry.toml with the generated status table regenerated, and the gate wired into CI. One commit per RFC so each derives r1 cleanly, which dogfoods the convention the RFC proposes. Two things the work found rather than sought. #17 is the proposal's own best argument - an RFC that proposed the canonical REQ registry, shipped, and was never numbered, so the RFC that built requirement tracking is itself untracked. And req-registry.py needs tomllib and on Python 3.9 reports 'inconclusive' while exiting 0, so it skipped silently on this host and what it skipped was a real fault in the branch: three requirements added without regenerating the table they appear in. Under a pinned 3.11 it failed immediately with STALE-GENERATED. PEP 723 headers now declare the interpreter floor on req-registry.py, reqs and rfc-check.py, on the principle that a gate which cannot run should fail rather than pass.

The anchor's migration tool is a source-to-source rewrite proved information-preserving by round-trip, not a parse-and-print. thermite-migrate.py rewrites in both directions so that to_v2(to_v3(x)) == x can be checked byte for byte on the real corpus - 67/67 files, including the 24 whose clause expressions wrap across lines. That check matters because the usual validation, re-certifying the corpus, cannot be run at all until a front end accepts the new surface. A clause runs from its keyword until its expression closes, tracked by delimiter balance, so a wrapped clause moves as one unit; keywords are recognised only at the head of a clause line, so an identifier named req in a body is untouched. Two design facts the round-trip forced out: the gap between keyword and expression must be preserved verbatim rather than re-aligned, because column-preserving arithmetic is not invertible once it clamps and alignment is a formatter's job; and the row must be restored before a measure rather than at the end, because fx is not last in the current grammar.

The anchor's implementation is scoped by measurement rather than estimate, in docs/rfcs/anchor-implementation.md. The compiler change is small and the test corpus is the schedule: five lexer keyword entries, five TokKind variants whose names do not change so the 53 downstream references stay put, one ordering change in parse_contract, two lines in the address allowlist, and clause names appearing as user-facing error strings. '!' already lexes as TokKind::Bang so the row needs a production rather than a new token. The volume is 619 clause lines embedded in 66 Rust files, which thermite-migrate.py does not reach because they sit inside string literals - the answer is a string-literal variant of the tool whose round-trip check applies unchanged, rather than 619 hand edits. Order: corpus first on a branch that does not build, then lexer and parser until the migrated corpus certifies, then addresses, then the embedded corpus, then regenerated goldens, then docs. And the migration and the parser change must be ONE PR, because no front end accepts the new surface until the parser moves, so a migrated corpus cannot certify on its own. The round-trip proof establishes the rewrite loses nothing; it does not establish the result means the same to the prover, and only re-certifying does.

Thermite 3 is being proposed upstream, and the motivation is reframed. The argument is Thermite's own stated purpose rather than Bulla's needs: the language is designed to be written principally by agents, and a surface built for that has requirements a human-authored one does not - a keyword's real cost is the prior it activates rather than the tokens it spends, and a clause read wrongly yields a vacuous proof rather than an error. fx, dec and inv are not merely terse, they point at effects, declarations and inverses. That gap between what the language is for and what it reads like is the whole of the anchor. Bulla's role is DISCOVERY rather than entitlement: a workload chosen to press hard enough to find where surface and capability run out, where every recorded gap was found by attempting something rather than reading the reference, and several contradicted the documentation in both directions. What that buys is evidence, not standing - Bulla has no verified subsystem, and a proposal earns its way on the design and the reproduction attached to it. Separately: the atproto RFC system is dropped as a direction; the file-based proposal in Thermite PR #127 is what we are using.
